implementation_notes: The standard library realizes the idiom directly: Cow<'a, B> is documented as a clone-on-write smart pointer that gives immutable access through Deref and clones the borrowed data lazily when to_mut() (or into_owned()) needs an owned value - the classic share-until-someone-writes shape, expressed as an enum of Borrowed(&'a B) and Owned rather than as a reference-counted handle. It is the tool for APIs that usually borrow (paths, strings, slices) but must occasionally own; the borrow checker replaces the count, so no detach can be forgotten at compile time.
pitfalls: Cow is clone-on-write, not mutate-in-place for borrowed data: every to_mut() on a still-borrowed value clones, so calling it repeatedly on copied Cow values copies repeatedly.
Cow demands B: ToOwned and pins the value to a lifetime; storing it in a long-lived struct infects the whole type with 'a where an owned field would be simpler.
Matching on Cow::Borrowed/Cow::Owned for control flow leaks the representation into callers; prefer Deref-based access.

variants.name: Arc::make_mut / Rc::make_mut (shared value, clone when shared)
variants.implementation_notes: For genuinely shared values (configuration, caches, state published to other threads) the Arc documentation states that Arc::make_mut provides clone-on-write semantics with efficient mutation without interior mutability: it clones the inner value only when the strong count is greater than one and otherwise mutates in place, so a writer pays the copy exactly while another handle still holds the old value. Arc is the thread-safe form (atomic count, higher overhead) and Rc the single-threaded counterpart; use Arc::get_mut when uniqueness is already guaranteed.
pitfalls: make_mut clones the whole inner value as soon as a second handle exists, so a write-heavy loop with a live snapshot copies per iteration; keep a single owner or use Mutex/RwLock.
The atomic count makes Arc itself thread-safe but does not make the inner value thread-safe: shared mutation still needs Mutex/RwLock.
Cycles of Arc handles leak - break back-edges with Weak.
